title: Entropy-balanced microbatch router for multi-GPU latency smoothing
creator: Aisha Patel
description: Introduce an entropy-balanced microbatch router that dynamically groups and routes inference requests across heterogeneous GPUs to smooth tail latency. The router combines token-wave quantile prediction with attention-aware kernel hints and NCCL coalescing windows to reduce blocking during prefill and decode phases without hurting average throughput. This ticket covers design, a prototype patch to the scheduler, integration tests, and a small benchmark suite comparing 1) baseline round-robin microbatching, 2) topology-aware token sharding, and 3) the new entropy-balanced router on a 4-GPU heterogeneous cluster (two A100s, two H100s).
acceptance_criteria: Router prototype merges to runtime/scheduler with feature flag --entropy-router
Tail P99 latency for mixed 8k/2k prompt workload reduced by >=15% vs baseline on target cluster
No regression in average token/sec throughput beyond 5% on stable synthetic loads
Integration tests for KV-cache affinity and canary fallback to round-robin pass in CI
Design doc updated with kernel-selection interaction and trade-offs
design_notes:
Core idea: compute a small per-request entropy score based on predicted token-wave variance (quantile model from recent traffic) and attention-memory footprint. Higher entropy (high variance predictions) exposures are routed to GPUs with larger headroom and more aggressive NCCL coalescing; low-entropy requests are packed to maximize kernel-fusion locality. Kernel-selection hints are passed to the executor so it can prefer fused attention kernels for low-entropy streams and streaming attention kernels for high-entropy streams. We avoid strict sharding by allowing soft-affinity and periodic rebalancing with watermarks. Safety: a fail-open fallback preserves existing scheduler behavior if the router detects instability.

Trade-offs considered: a) tighter affinity reduces NCCL setup overhead but can create hotspots; b) aggressive coalescing increases latency for single-token interactive requests. Decision: use quantile thresholds that adapt to recent SLO violations (feedback loop) and conservative coalescing for requests flagged interactive via metadata.

Kernel selection integration: router sends a kernel_hint tag (fused|streaming|mixed) with each microbatch to the runtime. Runtime chooses kernels based on hint and current sequence length distribution. This avoids expensive runtime introspection on every request and keeps control-plane overhead low.
